#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Host-package helpers for ./deploy. Sourced, never executed: sourcing is what
# lets ../tests/system-packages.sh drive these against a temp tree instead of
# /etc. Nothing here has an effect at source time, and every path is an
# argument -- no function reaches for a location of its own.
#
# SUDO is the privilege seam, and it is `${SUDO-sudo}`, not `${SUDO:-sudo}`:
# the tests set it to the empty string to mean "write as me", which the :-
# form would quietly turn back into sudo.

# Packages wanted on this host: the shared ./packages plus the optional
# per-host ./packages.<host>, which is how a box gets something the others
# have no business installing (steam on shiori and not on headless fujiwara).
#
# The format is one package per line with # comments, and the split is on any
# whitespace rather than per line: a two-names-on-one-line slip then fails as
# two packages pacman reports missing, instead of one concatenated name that
# silently never installs. Deduped, order preserved -- a name in both lists
# reaches pacman once, so the "installing missing" line stays readable.
#
# A missing per-host file is the normal case, not an error. The shared list's
# existence is ./deploy's check, because only deploy knows it is fatal there.
pacman_wants() { # pacman_wants <dir> <host>
  local dir=$1 host=$2 f
  for f in "$dir/packages" "$dir/packages.$host"; do
    # Quoted, so a host name containing a glob character is looked up
    # literally rather than expanded against the directory.
    [ -e "$f" ] || continue
    sed 's/#.*//' -- "$f"
  done | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | sed '/^$/d' | awk '!seen[$0]++'
}

# Append <line> to <conf> unless it is already there, and say so when it does.
# The one place this repo writes to a pacman-owned file: /etc/pacman.conf is a
# pacman backup file, so it cannot live under ./etc the way our override files
# do, and enabling a repo needs exactly one line in it. Everything that line
# pulls in stays in the repo, under ./etc/pacman.d/conf.d/.
#
#   • -qxF: whole line, fixed string. The stock pacman.conf ships commented
#     example Include lines, and a substring match would read one as "already
#     enabled" and never enable anything.
#   • the leading \n: an /etc file edited by hand may end without a newline,
#     and a blind append would glue the Include onto that last line. A blank
#     line in pacman.conf is inert.
#   • the echo: deploy's output is where a reader learns a root-owned file
#     outside this repo was edited. Silence on the no-op run is the point.
pacman_ensure_include() { # pacman_ensure_include <conf> <line>
  local conf=$1 line=$2
  grep -qxF -- "$line" "$conf" 2>/dev/null && return 0
  printf '\n%s\n' "$line" | ${SUDO-sudo} tee -a -- "$conf" >/dev/null
  echo "enabled in ${conf}: ${line}"
}

# Does <dbdir> hold a sync db for <repo>? Enabling a repo does not fetch one,
# and `pacman -S` against a repo with no db answers "target not found" -- which
# reads as a bad package name rather than as "you never synced". deploy checks
# this so it can say the real thing instead. It deliberately does not fix it:
# `pacman -Sy` without the -u is the partial-upgrade footgun deploy avoids
# everywhere else, so the cure is a human running `pacman -Syu`.
pacman_repo_synced() { # pacman_repo_synced <dbdir> <repo>
  [ -e "$1/$2.db" ]
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Run as your normal user (e.g. `mise run deploy`), NOT under sudo: the sops
# steps below decrypt with your GCP key under $HOME and each privileged install
# sudo's itself. Running the whole script as root points $HOME at /root, so sops
# can't find the key (and root has no KMS creds) -- fail fast instead.
if [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: run as your user (try 'mise run system:deploy'), not root." >&2
  exit 1
fi

cd "$(dirname "$0")"

# The list format, the per-host overlay and the one line we append to
# /etc/pacman.conf live in ./pacman.sh, so ../tests/system-packages.sh can drive
# them against a temp tree. Sourced for its functions; it does nothing on its own.
# shellcheck source=pacman.sh
. ./pacman.sh

# The sops credential selection and the decrypt-then-install pattern live in
# ./secrets.sh for the same reason, so ../tests/system-secrets.sh can drive them
# without touching /etc. Sourced for its functions; it does nothing on its own.
# shellcheck source=secrets.sh
. ./secrets.sh

# `uname -n`, not $HOSTNAME and not hostname(1): the kernel owns it where an env
# var is inheritable, the repo derives the host this way in three other places
# (home.nix's hms, two mise tasks), and hostname(1) lives in inetutils, which is
# installed on none of these boxes.
#
# Assigned here, at the top, and NOT inside the SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES else arm
# below where it used to live: the sops block near the end of this script reads
# $host too, so under `set -u` a SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES run aborted on an unbound
# variable after the etc/ copy and before every credential it installs. That
# flag exists to re-run the non-package half; it must not be the half that
# breaks. ../tests/system-secrets.sh checks the position.
host=$(uname -n); host=${host%%.*}

# ── host packages: converge pacman onto ./packages[.<host>] ──────────────────
# install-base.sh pacstraps the same list, but that only ever runs on the live
# ISO, so a package added after a host was built never reaches it.
#
# The order against the etc/ copy below does not matter for any file the copy
# writes, and it is worth saying so rather than inventing a reason: pacman owns
# NONE of the eight files that copy writes (`pacman -Qo` on each answers "No
# package owns"). The one exception is etc/pacman.d/conf.d/multilib.conf, which
# pacman must be able to read before this step runs `pacman -S`, so the multilib
# block below installs that single file itself rather than waiting. Everything under
# etc/ is an override path -- /etc/pam.d/polkit-1 shadows the polkit package's
# /usr/lib/pam.d/polkit-1, /etc/systemd/system/tailscaled.service shadows the
# packaged unit -- which is the mechanism that makes this whole directory work.
# Nor does the order spare any pam_fprintd load errors: every existing host has
# had that state since the polkit-1 stack was committed, and a fresh host
# pacstraps fprintd before deploy ever runs.
#
# An explicit host list, NOT `command -v pacman`: those are different
# predicates. kyuusaku is a box whose OS we do not own, and an Arch-based one
# would sail through a capability check and be handed a base metapackage.
# docs/new-host.md step 0 says to add a new host here. It happens to be the same
# four hosts as home.nix's `hms` case, but for an unrelated reason (that one
# means "has a Linux CI job"), so do not treat the two as one list -- kyuusaku
# is absent from both for different reasons, and a CI job would earn it a place
# in hms without earning one here.
#
# A host that is not listed still gets the etc/ copy below, so it keeps a
# pam_fprintd line it cannot load -- fail-safe (polkit falls through to the
# password) at the price of a log line per auth.
#
# A failure here WARNS and carries on rather than aborting: nothing later in
# this script is about packages, and the attic netrc further down is what lets
# the home-manager switch after it download CI's closure instead of compiling
# for an hour. Letting a stale mirror take that down would be a worse outcome
# than a host missing fprintd. SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES to any value skips the step
# outright -- tested for non-emptiness, so SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES=0 skips too.
#
# Without --noconfirm this step can PROMPT (pacman's "Proceed with installation?"),
# so a deploy driven over ssh wants a tty. Without one, pacman takes its defaults
# or aborts, and either way the warn-and-continue above keeps the rest running.
#
if [ -n "${SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES:-}" ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES set -- not touching pacman."
else
case "$host" in
utsuho | setsuna | shiori | fujiwara)
  # ── multilib: Arch's 32-bit repo, off by default ──────────────────────────
  # Needed by anything with a lib32- dependency; today that is steam, in
  # ./packages.shiori. Enabling a repo installs nothing on its own, so this
  # runs on every host here and the per-host list stays the only thing that
  # decides what a box actually gets.
  #
  # Why a drop-in instead of the obvious edit: /etc/pacman.conf is pacman's own
  # backup file. Copying it into etc/ would make this repo the owner of a file
  # pacman ships, and pacman's changes to it would start arriving as .pacnew
  # that nobody reads. So the repo owns the [multilib] section as a file of its
  # own under etc/pacman.d/conf.d/, and /etc/pacman.conf gets exactly one glob
  # Include -- appended once, whole-line matched, never rewritten. pacman
  # processes Include inline, so the section lands after [extra], which is
  # where Arch's own stock config puts multilib.
  #
  # The drop-in is installed here, not left to the etc/ copy further down: that
  # loop runs after `pacman -S`, and an Include whose glob matches nothing is
  # silently empty -- indistinguishable from multilib being off.
  sudo install -Dvm644 etc/pacman.d/conf.d/multilib.conf \
    /etc/pacman.d/conf.d/multilib.conf
  pacman_ensure_include /etc/pacman.conf 'Include = /etc/pacman.d/conf.d/*.conf'

  [ -r packages ] || { echo "system/deploy: ./packages is missing or unreadable" >&2; exit 1; }
  # The shared list plus this host's own ./packages.<host>, if it has one. See
  # ./pacman.sh for the format and why the split is on whitespace.
  mapfile -t want < <(pacman_wants . "$host")
  # mapfile returns 0 whatever the process substitution did, and neither `set
  # -e` nor pipefail sees inside one, so an empty parse has to be caught by
  # hand. Without this a renamed or emptied list makes this step a silent
  # no-op -- the exact failure the list was added to fix.
  [ ${#want[@]} -gt 0 ] || { echo "system/deploy: ./packages parsed to nothing" >&2; exit 1; }

  missing=()
  for p in "${want[@]}"; do
    # -Qq resolves virtual provides (`pacman -Qq sh` answers bash), so an entry
    # satisfied by a provider is not reported missing.
    pacman -Qq -- "$p" >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing+=("$p")
  done

  if [ ${#missing[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
    # Enabling multilib above does not fetch its db, and `pacman -S` against a
    # repo it has no db for says "target not found" -- which reads as a typo in
    # the list rather than as "you have never synced this repo". Say the real
    # thing. Not fixed here on purpose: the fix is `-Sy`, and refreshing without
    # upgrading is the partial-upgrade footgun the -S below is careful to avoid.
    if ! pacman_repo_synced /var/lib/pacman/sync multilib; then
      echo "system/deploy: multilib is enabled but has no sync db yet." >&2
      echo "  Run 'sudo pacman -Syu' first; until then nothing from it (steam," >&2
      echo "  any lib32-*) can resolve and pacman will call it a bad target." >&2
    fi
    echo "system/deploy: installing missing host packages: ${missing[*]}"
    # `--` because the list is data: a line starting with a dash would
    # otherwise be read as a pacman option (--hookdir=, --overwrite=, --root=),
    # and this runs under sudo.
    #
    # No `--noconfirm`, which answers every question with its default -- and the
    # default to "replace X with Y?" is yes. So a line here that reads as purely
    # additive could silently REMOVE a package from a running host by pulling in
    # something that replaces it. (Whether the separate "X conflicts with Y,
    # remove Y?" question also defaults to yes I did not confirm; it does not
    # change the conclusion.) Prompting costs a keypress, and only when something
    # is actually missing.
    #
    # No `-y` either: refreshing the db and then installing without upgrading is
    # the partial-upgrade footgun. `-S` against the db as it stands resolves the
    # version matching the libraries already installed, which is the safe
    # direction. It is not a guarantee -- if the db is already newer than the
    # system because something ran `pacman -Sy` by hand, installing anything
    # here drags its newer deps in and you get a partial upgrade through the
    # other door. Nothing this script can do about that; `-Syu` is the cure.
    #
    # Failure is a warning, not an abort (see the header): a stale db 404, a
    # held pacman lock, a refused sudo password, a full /var, an unresolvable
    # conflict. Any of them, and the rest of the deploy still runs.
    sudo pacman -S --needed -- "${missing[@]}" || {
      echo "system/deploy: pacman failed for: ${missing[*]}" >&2
      echo "  Common causes: a stale sync db (404 on a dropped version -- fix" >&2
      echo "  with 'sudo pacman -Syu'), another pacman holding the db lock, or" >&2
      echo "  no network. Continuing; nothing below needs these packages." >&2
    }
  fi

  # The step after convergence, for the one listed package that is a daemon:
  # `pacman -S` puts thermald's unit on disk without enabling or starting it, and
  # a package list has no way to say "and run it". ./thermald-setup is that half,
  # and it gates on the package being installed -- so which hosts get it stays a
  # question only ./packages.<host> answers (today, ./packages.shiori).
  #
  # Immediately after the install rather than further down: on the run that first
  # installs thermald, this is what makes the daemon actually run without waiting
  # for a reboot or a second deploy.
  #
  # Inside the SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES guard because it is the tail of the package
  # step -- skipping the convergence and then enabling what it would have
  # installed is not a state worth being able to reach.
  #
  # Warn rather than abort, for the same reason the pacman step above does:
  # nothing below this point wants thermald, and the attic netrc further down is
  # what spares the switch an hour of compiling.
  ./thermald-setup || echo "system/deploy: thermald-setup failed; continuing." >&2
  ;;
*)
  echo "system/deploy: ${host} is not one of our Arch hosts -- skipping host packages."
  ;;
esac
fi

find etc/ -type d | while read -r d; do sudo mkdir -p "/${d}"; done
find etc/ -type f | while read -r f; do sudo cp -v "${f}" "/${f}"; done

# polkit only scans /usr/share/polkit-1/actions for action definitions, which
# etc/ can't reach; install Bitwarden's unlock action there so its "system
# authentication" biometric prompt is authorized on this non-NixOS host.
sudo install -Dvm644 polkit-1/actions/com.bitwarden.Bitwarden.policy \
  /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/com.bitwarden.Bitwarden.policy

# ── gnome-keyring: let the home-manager unit own the daemon ───────────────────
# The login collection can only be unlocked at daemon startup, so home-manager
# runs its own gnome-keyring.service whose ExecStart unseals the passphrase from
# the TPM (see gnome-keyring-tpm in home.nix). Mask Arch's packaged units so a
# second, *locked* daemon can't be started behind our back -- its socket unit
# listens on %t/keyring/control and would socket-activate one on any control-op.
# This is only half the job: the D-Bus activation files in /usr/share also start
# a locked daemon, and systemd masking does nothing about those. They are
# shadowed from ~/.local/share/dbus-1/services by home.nix.
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/user/sockets.target.wants/gnome-keyring-daemon.socket
sudo ln -sfn /dev/null /etc/systemd/user/gnome-keyring-daemon.socket
sudo ln -sfn /dev/null /etc/systemd/user/gnome-keyring-daemon.service

# Unsealing the gnome-keyring passphrase reads /dev/tpmrm0, which is root:tss 0660.
# Takes effect at next login, not in the current session.
if ! id -nG "$USER" | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -qx tss; then
  sudo gpasswd -a "$USER" tss
fi

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
# systemd-oomd parses oomd.conf (and its drop-ins) once at startup, so a changed
# etc/systemd/oomd.conf.d/* must be followed by an actual restart. `enable --now`
# is NOT enough: --now only *starts* a stopped unit, so on a host where oomd is

# `restart` covers both cases (starts it if stopped) and kills nothing on its way
# through -- oomd holds no state worth preserving across a reload.

# nix.custom.conf adds attic.ko.ag/kube as an extra substituter; the cache is
# PRIVATE, so the nix daemon needs a read token. We are not a nix `trusted-user`,
# so both the config and the token must reach the daemon at the system level.
#
#   • Determinate Nix auto-`!include`s nix.custom.conf from /etc/nix/nix.conf and
#     merges /etc/determinate/netrc.custom (via config.json) into its netrc.
#   • Plain upstream nix (e.g. utsuho) does neither, so we wire it up here:
#       - ensure /etc/nix/nix.conf `!include`s nix.custom.conf (idempotent)
#       - render the token to /etc/nix/netrc, the daemon's default netrc-file
#     (On a Determinate host the extra /etc/nix/netrc copy is simply unused.)
# The token is sops-encrypted in ../secrets.yaml: decrypt as the user (GCP KMS),
# then install to /etc as root. The token is never printed.
#
# Which credential that decrypt uses is per-host and is decided in home.nix, not
# here: a WIF host signs a short-lived JWT with a local key and has no decryption
# key on disk at all, while every other host still has the GCP service-account
# key under $HOME. This used to hardcode the service-account path, which meant it
# could never decrypt on the WIF host -- and because the failure landed inside a
# pipeline, it presented as an empty netrc rather than as an error. ./secrets.sh
# reads the decision back out of the flake so there is only ever one copy of it.
#
# An explicit GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS still wins, for the case where you
# are deliberately deploying with some other credential. ./secrets.sh owns that
# choice -- including the deliberate refusal to turn ALLOW_EXECUTABLES on for an
# override, which is a code-execution interlock and not a compatibility flag; the
# reasoning is written out there.
[ -z "${GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS-}" ] \
  || echo "system/deploy: using GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS from the environment"

# and these lines are KEY=VALUE pairs meant for `export`, not for the shell.
#
# No `||` on the mapfile, deliberately. mapfile's exit status is mapfile's own
# and never the process substitution's -- the same trap the pacman_wants call
# above documents -- so a `|| exit` there would be dead code claiming a check it
# does not perform. A failed `nix eval` writes to stderr and nothing to stdout,
# so it arrives here as an empty array, which the length test catches.
mapfile -t sops_env < <(sops_env_select .. "$host")

# zero words, and bare `export` prints the whole environment and succeeds.
[ "${#sops_env[@]}" -gt 0 ] || {
  echo "system/deploy: no sops.environment for $host — nix eval failed, or the host has none." >&2
  echo "system/deploy: nix's own error, if any, is above." >&2
  exit 1
}
export "${sops_env[@]}"

# Fail here, with the reason, rather than four lines down inside a decrypt. On a
# WIF host this is a store path from the flake, so it is missing exactly when the
# home-manager generation that provides it has not been built yet.
if [ ! -r "$GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS" ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: credential config not readable: $GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS" >&2
  echo "system/deploy: run 'hms' first (it builds that path), then re-run this." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Plain upstream nix only reads /etc/nix/nix.conf; pull in nix.custom.conf so the
# substituter + trusted key take effect. Idempotent, and a no-op on Determinate
# (whose own nix.conf already includes it, so the grep matches and we skip).
if ! sudo grep -qF 'nix.custom.conf' /etc/nix/nix.conf 2>/dev/null; then
  echo '!include nix.custom.conf' | sudo tee -a /etc/nix/nix.conf >/dev/null
fi

install_secret ../secrets.yaml atticPullToken /etc/determinate/netrc.custom 'machine attic.ko.ag password '
install_secret ../secrets.yaml atticPullToken /etc/nix/netrc 'machine attic.ko.ag password '

# ── remote builder: SSH key the nix daemon uses to reach mari ─────────────────
# nix.custom.conf delegates aarch64-darwin builds to sauyon@mari-1 over Tailscale;
# the daemon (root) authenticates with this key. Private key is sops-encrypted in
# ../secrets.yaml; install root-owned, 0600. Never printed.
install_secret ../secrets.yaml mariBuilderKey /etc/nix/mari-builder-key

# Pick up the new substituter, trusted key, netrc, and builder.
sudo systemctl restart nix-daemon

# ── tailscaled: patched build from this flake (Linux only) ───────────────────
# Tailscale SSH calls logind CreateSession before the user's shell runs, so for a
# systemd-homed user whose LUKS home is still locked it starts user@<uid>.service
# against homed's fallback home ("/") and permanently breaks that user manager's
# unit search path for the rest of the boot. The patch makes tailscaled ask homed
# for the user's state first and skip session creation when the home isn't active.
# See ../patches/tailscale-ssh-skip-logind-session-for-locked-homed-user.patch
#
# Build as the invoking user (root's nix may lack flakes and our substituters),
# then have root pin the result. A symlink placed directly in /nix/var/nix/gcroots
# is a permanent GC root, and we reuse it as the stable path tailscaled.service
# references -- it must resolve at boot, i.e. outside the encrypted home.
if [[ "$(uname -s)" == Linux ]]; then
  ts_out="$(nix build --no-link --print-out-paths "$(cd .. && pwd)#tailscale-patched")"
  sudo ln -sfn "${ts_out}" /nix/var/nix/gcroots/tailscale-patched
  # The CLI too: /usr/bin/tailscale belongs to the distro package, which this
  # replaces. The wrapper dispatches on argv[0], so a symlink named `tailscale`
  # gets CLI behaviour rather than the daemon.
  sudo install -d /usr/local/bin
  sudo ln -sfn /nix/var/nix/gcroots/tailscale-patched/bin/tailscale /usr/local/bin/tailscale
  sudo systemctl daemon-reload
  sudo systemctl restart tailscaled
fi

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Enable thermald where it is installed, and nowhere else.
#
# The split of labour with ./packages.<host>: that list decides WHICH hosts want
# thermald (today only ./packages.shiori), and ./deploy's pacman step installs
# it. This script does the one thing a package list cannot express -- `pacman -S`
# puts a unit on disk, it does not start it or wire it into a target, and
# install-base.sh's `systemctl enable` line runs once inside the chroot of a
# fresh install, so it only ever reaches the NEXT new host. That gap is how
# fprintd stayed uninstalled for months; a daemon nobody enabled is the same gap
# with the same shape.
#
# So the gate here is "is thermald installed", not the CPU vendor. Deliberately:
# a vendor check here would be a second, independent answer to a question the
# per-host list already answers, and the two would drift. thermald is Intel-only
# -- it steers the ACPI DPTF devices (int3400/int3403) and the
# processor_thermal_device RAPL knobs, and exits on anything else -- but that is
# an argument about which list it belongs in, which is settled in the list.
#
# WHY thermald AT ALL: it is the Framework/Intel recommendation, not a hunch.
# ArchWiki's Framework Laptop 13 page ("Lowering fan noise") names it for the
# Intel version specifically; both distributions Framework certifies the Laptop
# 13 Pro against -- Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and Fedora 44 -- ship it by default on
# Intel; and Phoronix ran its Panther Lake performance-profile numbers with
# thermald applied. shiori is a Framework Laptop 13 Pro (Core Ultra X7 358H,
# Panther Lake) and has the int3400/int3403 devices thermald steers.
#
# It coexists with power-profiles-daemon rather than replacing it: ppd sets the
# EPP and the ACPI platform_profile, thermald manages the passive trip points and
# fan response underneath. That pairing is what Fedora and Ubuntu both ship.
#
# Seams, for ../tests/thermald-setup.sh: pacman, sudo and systemctl are resolved
# through PATH, so the harness stubs them and no case needs a real package, a
# real unit, or root.
set -euo pipefail

# The host asked for thermald by listing it, or it did not. Nothing to do is the
# normal case on three of four hosts, and it has to be silent -- a deploy step
# that narrates its own no-op on every run trains people to skim the output.
if ! pacman -Qq thermald >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  exit 0
fi

# is-enabled/is-active are unprivileged where `enable --now` is not, so asking
# first is what keeps a converged host at zero sudo prompts. ./deploy runs on
# every `mise run system:deploy`; a step that escalated unconditionally would
# turn the password prompt into background noise.
#
# Both halves matter. Enabled-but-stopped is a live host where someone ran
# `systemctl stop`; active-but-disabled is one that loses the daemon at the next
# reboot. Either way `enable --now` is the same idempotent fix.
if [ "$(systemctl is-enabled thermald.service 2>/dev/null)" != enabled ] ||
  [ "$(systemctl is-active thermald.service 2>/dev/null)" != active ]; then
  echo "system/thermald-setup: enabling thermald.service"
  sudo systemctl enable --now thermald.service
fi

  STUB_INSTALLED=0 STUB_ENABLED=disabled STUB_ACTIVE=inactive -- \
  +"systemctl enable --now thermald.service" +"sudo"

  STUB_INSTALLED=0 STUB_ENABLED=enabled STUB_ACTIVE=active -- \
  -"sudo" +"systemctl is-enabled thermald.service"

# Both halves of the check earn their keep, and they fail differently: enabled-
# but-stopped is a live host where someone ran `systemctl stop`, active-but-
# disabled is one that silently loses the daemon at the next reboot.
run_case "enabled but stopped: re-enables" 0 \
  STUB_INSTALLED=0 STUB_ENABLED=enabled STUB_ACTIVE=inactive -- \
  +"systemctl enable --now thermald.service"
run_case "running but disabled: re-enables" 0 \
  STUB_INSTALLED=0 STUB_ENABLED=disabled STUB_ACTIVE=active -- \
  +"systemctl enable --now thermald.service"

# one. This is what would break if the checks were ever loosened to "not

run_case "unknown unit state: still tries to enable" 0 \
  STUB_INSTALLED=0 STUB_ENABLED=masked STUB_ACTIVE=failed -- \
  +"systemctl enable --now thermald.service"

# system/deploy's `|| echo ... continuing` print, rather than the deploy
# reporting success over a daemon that never started.
run_case "enable failure is reported" 1 \
  STUB_INSTALLED=0 STUB_ENABLED=disabled STUB_ACTIVE=inactive STUB_ENABLE_RC=1 -- \
  +"systemctl enable --now thermald.service"

echo
if [ "$fails" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "all $n cases passed"
else
  echo "$fails of $n cases FAILED"
fi
exit $((fails > 0))

# TDD

## Overview

**Test-first, always.** Write the failing test before the code it covers, watch
it fail, then write the minimal code to make it pass. A test you never saw fail
proves nothing — it may pass for the wrong reason, or not exercise the behavior
at all.

Keep the test scoped to the interfaces you are actually changing — a test that
drifts wider stops being a contract anyone can rely on. Inside a drovr phase
this also binds the next phase's contract.

## The cycle

1. **RED** — write the failing test named in the task's verification. Run it.
   *Watch it fail*, and confirm it fails for the reason you expect (missing
   behavior, not a typo or compile error elsewhere).
2. **GREEN** — write the *minimal* code to make that test pass. No extra
   features, no speculative abstraction — just enough to go green.
3. **REFACTOR** — clean up with the test as your safety net, re-running it.

Repeat per behavior. One failing test at a time.

## Red flags — STOP

- Wrote code before the test → delete it, start with the test.
- "I'll add the test after" → tests-after check *what the code does*, not what it
  *should* do. Test first.
- Test passed the first time you ran it → you never saw RED; make sure it truly
  exercises the new behavior.
- Test is scoped wider than this task's interfaces → tighten it; drift breaks the
  contract the next phase inherits.

## Verifying the pass

Green on the one test is necessary, not sufficient. Before claiming done, hand
off to `drovr:verification-before-completion` — run the full suite and the build,
and confirm with evidence, not assertion.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for system/aur-setup, the AUR-helper bootstrap system/deploy runs beside
# its package convergence. They drive the real script with stub
# pacman/git/makepkg/sudo/id on PATH, so no case clones from the AUR, builds a
# package, needs root, or touches this machine.
#
# What is being protected here:
#
#   The gate, and its silence. A host that already has paru takes this path on
#   every single `mise run system:deploy` -- so it must do nothing and say
#   nothing, and in particular must never reach git or sudo. A deploy step that
#   narrated a no-op, or escalated to do one, is how output stops being read and
#   how the password prompt becomes background noise (the same assertion
#   ./thermald-setup.sh makes, for the same reason).
#
#   The gate is on `paru`, not on `paru-bin`. pacman -Qq resolves provides, so a
#   host where someone built the from-source `paru` is already served -- and
#   installing paru-bin over it would replace a package the human chose.
#
#   Build hygiene. makepkg must run as the user (it refuses as root, with a
#   message that reads like a bug), in a throwaway directory that is gone
#   afterwards, and never in this repo.
#
#   Failure is loud. Every failure path must leave a non-zero status, because
#   that is the only thing that makes system/deploy's `|| echo ... continuing`
#   print instead of the deploy reporting success over a host with no helper.
#
#   ./tests/aur-setup.sh                 # tests system/aur-setup
#   ./tests/aur-setup.sh /path/to/script # tests one you already have
set -u

SCRIPT="${1:-$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../system" && pwd)/aur-setup}"
[ -x "$SCRIPT" ] || { echo "not executable: $SCRIPT" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $SCRIPT"

D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0

# --- stubs -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Each records its argv in $CALLS and answers from a STUB_* variable, so a case
# reads as "what the host looks like" rather than as a script of mocks.
mkdir -p "$D/bin"

# Two queries, two answers. Keyed on the package name rather than on call order:
# the script is free to ask in either order, and a positional stub would pin an
# ordering the script never promised.
cat > "$D/bin/pacman" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "pacman $*" >> "$CALLS"
if [ "$1" = -Qq ]; then
  case "${*: -1}" in
  paru)       exit "${STUB_HAVE_PARU:-1}" ;;
  base-devel) exit "${STUB_HAVE_BASE_DEVEL:-0}" ;;
  *)          exit 1 ;;
  esac
fi
exit 0
EOF

# `clone` populates the destination the way a real one would, so the script's
# own cd/rev-parse/makepkg steps have something to work with. A failing clone
# leaves nothing behind -- which is what a real network failure looks like.
cat > "$D/bin/git" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "git $*" >> "$CALLS"
case "$1" in
clone)
  [ "${STUB_CLONE_RC:-0}" = 0 ] || exit "${STUB_CLONE_RC}"
  dest=${*: -1}
  mkdir -p "$dest"
  echo '# stub PKGBUILD' > "$dest/PKGBUILD"
  ;;
-C) echo "${STUB_AUR_COMMIT:-d15ea5e}" ;;
esac
exit 0
EOF

# Records the directory it was run in as well as its argv: "built in a throwaway
# dir, not in the repo" is an assertion no argv can carry.
cat > "$D/bin/makepkg" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "makepkg $*" >> "$CALLS"
printf '%s\n' "$PWD" > "$BUILDDIR_RECORD"
exit "${STUB_MAKEPKG_RC:-0}"
EOF

# Not `exec "$@"` blindly: recording the sudo itself is what lets the converged
# case assert that this step never escalates to do nothing.
cat > "$D/bin/sudo" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "sudo $*" >> "$CALLS"
exec "$@"
EOF

# So a case can present itself as root without being root.
cat > "$D/bin/id" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
[ "$1" = -u ] && { echo "${STUB_UID:-1000}"; exit 0; }
exec /usr/bin/id "$@"
EOF

chmod +x "$D/bin"/*

# --- runner ------------------------------------------------------------------
# want_rc, then leading VAR=value arguments for the case, then `--` and a list of
# "+needle" (must appear in the call log), "-needle" (must not), "out:" (no
# output at all) and "out:needle" (output must contain it).
run_case() { # desc want_rc [VAR=val ...] -- [+/-needle | out:[needle] ...]
  local desc=$1 want_rc=$2; shift 2
  local env=() rc out
  while [ $# -gt 0 ] && [ "$1" != -- ]; do env+=("$1"); shift; done

  : > "$D/calls"
  : > "$D/builddir"

  rc=$?

  local bad=() needle
  [ "$rc" = "$want_rc" ] || bad+=("exit $rc, wanted $want_rc")
  for needle in "$@"; do
    case "$needle" in
    out:) [ -z "$out" ] || bad+=("wanted no output, got: $out") ;;
    out:*) case "$out" in *"${needle#out:}"*) ;; *) bad+=("output lacks: ${needle#out:}") ;; esac ;;

    -*) grep -qF -- "${needle#-}" "$D/calls" && bad+=("unwanted call: ${needle#-}") ;;
    esac
  done

  if [ ${#bad[@]} -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "ok   $desc"
  else
    fails=$((fails + 1))
    echo "FAIL $desc"
    printf '       %s\n' "${bad[@]}"
    printf '       calls: %s\n' "$(tr '\n' '; ' < "$D/calls")"
    [ -n "$out" ] && printf '       output: %s\n' "$out"
  fi
}

# A bare assertion for the things that outlive a run -- the build directory in
# particular, which can only be judged after the script's own EXIT trap has run.
check() { # check <desc> <condition-as-args...>
  n=$((n + 1))
  local desc=$1; shift
  if "$@"; then
    echo "ok   $desc"
  else
    fails=$((fails + 1))
    echo "FAIL $desc"
    printf '       failed: %s\n' "$*"
  fi
}

# --- the gate ----------------------------------------------------------------
# The converged host, which is every host after its first deploy. Nothing may
# happen: no clone, no build, and above all no sudo, or every deploy from here on
# asks for a password to do nothing.
run_case "paru present: does nothing" 0 STUB_HAVE_PARU=0 -- \
  +"pacman -Qq paru" -"git" -"makepkg" -"sudo"

run_case "paru present: says nothing" 0 STUB_HAVE_PARU=0 -- out:

# The gate names the provides, not the package, so a from-source `paru` counts.
# pacman -Qq answers for either; what matters is that the script asks about
# `paru` and never about `paru-bin`, which only paru-bin itself would satisfy.
run_case "gate asks for the provides, not paru-bin" 0 STUB_HAVE_PARU=0 -- \
  +"pacman -Qq paru" -"pacman -Qq paru-bin"

# --- the bootstrap -----------------------------------------------------------
# The first deploy on a host with no helper: clone the AUR package, build it,
# install it. Over https to aur.archlinux.org -- the `aur` ssh alias in home.nix
# is for pushing one's own packages and authenticates as a user this host has no
# key for.
run_case "paru absent: clones and builds paru-bin" 0 STUB_HAVE_PARU=1 -- \
  +"https://aur.archlinux.org/paru-bin.git" +"makepkg -si"

# What was built is a moving target -- the AUR's master, whatever it says today.
# Printing the commit is the only record of which one this host got.
run_case "reports the AUR commit it built" 0 \
  STUB_HAVE_PARU=1 STUB_AUR_COMMIT=c0ffee1 -- out:c0ffee1

# No --noconfirm, for the reason system/deploy spells out for its own `pacman
# -S`: the default answer to "replace X with Y?" is yes, so a step that answers
# every question with its default can remove a package from a running host.
run_case "does not pass --noconfirm" 0 STUB_HAVE_PARU=1 -- -"noconfirm"

# The build happens in a throwaway directory and that directory is gone
# afterwards -- a PKGBUILD, a source tarball and a built package left in the repo
# or in $HOME is litter that the next `git status` reads as uncommitted work.
run_case "builds outside the repo" 0 STUB_HAVE_PARU=1 -- +"makepkg -si"
built=$(cat "$D/builddir")
repo=$(cd "$(dirname "$SCRIPT")/.." && pwd)
check "build dir is not in the repo" [ "${built#"$repo"}" = "$built" ]
check "build dir is cleaned up" [ ! -e "$built" ]

# --- preconditions -----------------------------------------------------------
# makepkg refuses to run as root, with a message about PKGBUILDs and fakeroot
# that reads like a bug in the PKGBUILD rather than like "you used sudo". Say the
# real thing, and say it before a clone happens as root and leaves root-owned
# files in a temp dir.
run_case "refuses to run as root" 1 STUB_HAVE_PARU=1 STUB_UID=0 -- \
  -"git" -"makepkg" out:root

# base-devel supplies fakeroot and the rest of makepkg's toolchain. It is
# pacstrapped by install/packages-install-only and deliberately not enforced
# after that, so a host can genuinely be without it -- and makepkg's own failure
# for a missing fakeroot arrives deep in a build log.
run_case "no base-devel: refuses before cloning" 1 \
  STUB_HAVE_PARU=1 STUB_HAVE_BASE_DEVEL=1 -- \
  -"git" -"makepkg" out:base-devel

# --- failure -----------------------------------------------------------------
# Both failure paths have to leave non-zero, so system/deploy's
# `|| echo ... continuing` prints. A clone that failed must not be built from.
run_case "clone failure is reported" 1 STUB_HAVE_PARU=1 STUB_CLONE_RC=128 -- \
  +"git clone" -"makepkg"

run_case "build failure is reported" 1 STUB_HAVE_PARU=1 STUB_MAKEPKG_RC=1 -- \
  +"makepkg -si"

# ...and a failed build still leaves nothing behind. A half-built package tree in
# a temp dir is the case where a trap is easiest to get wrong.
failed_build=$(cat "$D/builddir")
check "build dir is cleaned up after a failure" [ ! -e "$failed_build" ]

echo
if [ "$fails" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "all $n cases passed"
else
  echo "$fails of $n cases FAILED"
fi
exit $((fails > 0))

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Bootstrap the AUR helper -- paru-bin -- on a host that has none.
#
# WHY THIS IS A SCRIPT AND NOT A LINE IN ./packages: paru is not in any pacman
# repo. ./deploy's convergence ends in `pacman -S`, so a `paru-bin` line in
# ./packages would be reported missing on every host on every deploy and answered
# with "target not found" -- which reads as a typo in the list. The AUR is a
# recipe host, not a repo: getting a package from it means cloning a PKGBUILD and
# running makepkg, and that is the whole of what this script does.
#
# WHY NOT home.nix, WHICH IS WHERE ANYTHING A USER CAN OWN BELONGS: nixpkgs does
# package paru, and it would even run -- it shells out to pacman and makepkg from
# PATH. But paru links libalpm.so, pacman's own library, whose soname bumps with
# pacman. nixpkgs would build it against nixpkgs' pacman, and the first time the
# two versions drift the helper stops loading on a host whose pacman is fine. A
# thing that links the host package manager's library has to be built against the
# host's copy of it, so it is a host package -- one of the "a user profile cannot
# provide it" cases ./packages describes, which happens not to be installable the
# way the rest of that list is.
#
# WHY paru-bin RATHER THAN paru: the -bin package is the upstream release binary,
# so a rebuild is a download. Building paru from source pulls a Rust toolchain
# and compiles it -- on every update, on every host, for a program whose releases
# upstream already publishes built.
#
# WHAT YOU ARE TRUSTING, stated plainly because a makepkg run is arbitrary code
# execution as this user: the AUR maintainer's PKGBUILD. makepkg verifies the
# release tarball against the sha256sums recorded in that PKGBUILD, which means
# the checksum and the URL are trusted from the same place -- it protects against
# a corrupted download, not against the AUR account. That is the AUR's model
# whether you use this script or type the commands, and it is the reason this
# installs exactly one package (a helper) rather than becoming a general AUR
# package list. If a second AUR package is ever wanted, it is paru's job by then.
#
# Unpinned, deliberately: this clones the AUR master rather than a fixed commit.
# A pin would buy nothing here -- paru updates *itself* from the AUR the moment it
# exists, so a pinned bootstrap installs a stale paru that immediately replaces
# itself, and the pin then needs bumping forever for no gain. What the pin would
# have given is a record of what was built, so the script prints the commit.
#
# Seams, for ../tests/aur-setup.sh: pacman, git, makepkg, sudo and id are
# resolved through PATH, so the harness stubs them and no case clones from the
# AUR, builds a package, or needs root.
set -euo pipefail

pkg=paru-bin

# Already served, which is every host after its first deploy. Silent: ./deploy
# runs on every `mise run system:deploy`, and a step that narrates its own no-op
# trains people to skim the output.
#
# The query is `paru`, not `paru-bin`. -Qq resolves virtual provides, and paru-bin
# provides paru -- so this also answers yes on a host where someone built the
# from-source `paru`. That host is served too, and installing paru-bin over it
# would replace a package a human deliberately chose.
if pacman -Qq paru >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  exit 0
fi

# makepkg refuses to run as root, and says so in terms of PKGBUILDs and fakeroot
# that read like a bug in the recipe rather than "you used sudo". Say the real
# thing, and say it before a clone runs as root and leaves root-owned files
# behind. ./deploy already refuses as root for its own reasons; this is for a
# hand-run of just this script.
if [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "system/aur-setup: run as your user, not root -- makepkg refuses to run as root." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# base-devel is fakeroot and the rest of makepkg's toolchain. It is pacstrapped
# by ../install/packages-install-only and deliberately never re-enforced, so a
# host can genuinely be without it -- and makepkg's complaint about a missing
# fakeroot arrives partway through a build.
if ! pacman -Qq base-devel >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "system/aur-setup: base-devel is not installed; makepkg needs it (fakeroot)." >&2
  echo "  Run 'sudo pacman -S --needed base-devel', then re-run this." >&2
  exit 1
fi

# A throwaway directory, removed however this exits. Not ./ and not $HOME: what a
# makepkg leaves behind is a source tarball, a src/ tree and a built package, and
# in the repo that is litter the next `git status` reads as uncommitted work.
build=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$build"' EXIT

echo "system/aur-setup: no AUR helper installed; building ${pkg} from the AUR"

# https, not the `aur` ssh alias in home.nix: that alias is for pushing one's own
# packages and authenticates as a user this host has no key for.
#
# A full clone rather than --depth 1. An AUR package repo is a few kilobytes, so
# shallow saves nothing measurable and adds a way for the one-shot bootstrap on a
# new host to fail.
git clone "https://aur.archlinux.org/${pkg}.git" "$build/$pkg"
echo "system/aur-setup: ${pkg} at AUR commit $(git -C "$build/$pkg" rev-parse --short HEAD)"

cd "$build/$pkg"

# -s resolves the PKGBUILD's own dependencies through pacman (that is what sudo's
# itself), -i installs the package it built.
#
# No --noconfirm, for the reason ./deploy spells out for its `pacman -S`: it
# answers every question with its default, and the default to "replace X with Y?"
# is yes -- so a step that looks purely additive can remove a package from a
# running host. This prompts, once per host, ever.
makepkg -si

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions. The first names its addressee; the rest hold for anyone.

- **Never run a reviewer in the background — you, the agent in a herdr pane,
  where ending a turn *is* how you report done.** Do not set
  `run_in_background`, do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is
  out. A backgrounded reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a
  finished turn, and the run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it
  blocking and read its verdict in the turn you dispatched it. That reason is
  role-specific, so there is exactly one role it does not bind: the **driver**,
  which backgrounds the panel and ends the turn because its harness re-invokes
  it on process exit — `skills/pipeline/SKILL.md` says so at its own loop. A
  split by role, not a preference. In a pane, the prohibition is yours.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path, then classify the round by how the panel exited:

   | Exit | What it means |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | clean — a real range was reviewed, nothing blocking |
   | 3 | blocking findings; go to step 5 |
   | 2 | timeout — reviewers are slow, not broken. Re-run the same command: it resumes the panel in flight |
   | 1 | error, or an empty `<base>..HEAD` it refused. Fix the range or the setup; never re-run blindly |
   | 137/143 | **your own harness killed it.** drovr produced no verdict at all, and none of the rows above describes the run. Re-run to resume, and record the round as **unclassifiable** — never as a timeout |

   A reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the five: re-dispatch rather
   than report its silence.

   **Only 0 is clean, and one clean round does not end the loop.** Stop at
   whichever of three comes first:
   - **Two consecutive clean rounds over an unchanged HEAD.** Any edit between
     them resets the count — the second round is evidence about the first only
     if it read the same code.
   - **A cap of six rounds**, which is *not* a clean ending: write up every
     round's verdict and everything still open (step 5), and finish on that
     record rather than on a verdict. Only rounds that delivered every
     configured angle count toward the cap — a missing angle is a Critical
     stand-in, so a round that lost a reviewer never measured the code.
   - **Two consecutive rounds that lost a dimension** — its own outcome,
     neither clean nor the cap: the panel is failing to deliver and further
     rounds are not measuring the code. Name the angles that never ran. Without
     this the loop cannot end at all, since such a round is never clean and
     never counts toward the cap.

   Three caveats the rule owes you. Two cleans make a false clean **less
   likely**, not unlikely, and prove nothing about convergence — in forge#88's
   own data two consecutive cleans preceded a `changes` round with seven
   findings. **Six is a starting number, revisable on evidence**, not a
   principled constant. And every word of this is prose nothing enforces — the
   shape of the *"re-run it"* that produced 47 re-arms over 14 hours.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral with
   `drovr code-review defer`.** Per finding: quote it, then name the edit
   answering it by file — or, if you are not making it, run

   ```
   drovr code-review defer <RUN> <TASK> --file <path> [--line <n>] \
     --severity <critical|important|nit> --summary "<the finding>" \
     --reason "<why it is not being fixed>"
   ```

   A deferral written only in prose is one the next round cannot read, so it
   re-raises the finding you already ruled on. The command appends to a
   per-task log every later seed carries; prose does not.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`. **Done is
   step 3's termination rule met, not the first exit 0** — say which of the
   three ended it, and on the cap or a lost dimension say plainly that the loop
   ended on a record rather than on a clean verdict.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

One read away, in `skills/code-review/worked-example.md`: a 320-line spec, a
client call in 19 minutes, a $45,000 sign-off and a lead writing *"just send
it"* — the rationalization refused, the panel run, two Importants found, the
call moved 22 minutes. Worth reading once; the rules above do not depend on it.

aur: a helper on every Arch host, since pacman -S cannot install one

`mise run system:deploy` converges pacman onto system/packages, and that
step structurally cannot reach paru: the AUR is a recipe host, not a repo,
so a `paru-bin` line in that list would be reported missing on every host
on every deploy and answered with "target not found" -- which reads as a
typo in the list rather than as "this is not that kind of package".

So system/aur-setup is the shape system/thermald-setup already established
for the other thing a package list cannot express: deploy calls it right
after the convergence, inside the four-host arm, and it clones the PKGBUILD
and runs `makepkg -si` once per host.

It gates on `pacman -Qq paru` -- the provides, not the package name. paru-bin
declares `provides=('paru')` and `conflicts=('paru')`, so asking about
paru-bin would mean a host with a from-source paru gets a makepkg that ends
in pacman offering to remove a package a human deliberately chose. Every
host after its first deploy takes the gate, silently and with no sudo: a
step that narrated its no-op, or escalated to do one, is how deploy's output
stops being read.

Why paru-bin and not nixpkgs' paru, which does exist and would even run:
paru links libalpm.so and depends on it by versioned soname (`libalpm.so>=14`
today). Built against nixpkgs' pacman it breaks the first time the two
versions drift, on a host whose own pacman is fine. Anything linking the host
package manager's library is a host package.

Why paru-bin and not paru: the -bin package is upstream's release binary, so
an update is a download rather than a Rust toolchain and a compile, on every
host, every time.

Unpinned on purpose. paru updates itself from the AUR the moment it exists,
so a pinned bootstrap would install a stale paru that immediately replaces
itself, and the pin would need bumping forever for nothing. What a pin would
have given is a record of what was built, so the script prints the commit.

What is being trusted is stated in the script: the AUR maintainer's PKGBUILD.
makepkg checks the release tarball against sha256sums recorded in that same
PKGBUILD, so it covers a corrupted download, not the AUR account. That is why
this installs exactly one package -- a helper -- rather than growing into a
general AUR package list. A second AUR package is paru's job by then.

tests/aur-setup.sh drives the real script with stub pacman/git/makepkg/sudo/id
over 14 cases: the silent converged path, the refusals before anything is
cloned (root, because makepkg's own complaint reads like a bug in the recipe;
no base-devel, which install/packages-install-only pacstraps and never
re-enforces), that the build happens in a throwaway directory outside the repo
and is removed on both the success and the failure path, and that each failure
propagates the failing tool's own status -- which is what makes deploy's
`|| echo ... continuing` print instead of a deploy reporting success over a
host with no helper.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for STEAM_FORCE_DESKTOPUI_SCALING, the one lever that makes the Steam
# client legible on a host whose compositor scale it cannot see.
#
# Steam's desktop UI is CEF, and it is an X11 client. hyprland.nix sets
# xwayland.force_zero_scaling, so on a scaled panel every X11 client gets the
# full pixel grid and no DPI hint -- the documented "crisp and small over blurry"
# trade. Steam ignores Xft.dpi and GDK_DPI_SCALE, so the only way back to a
# correct size is to hand CEF its own scale factor, which it lays out at rather
# than bitmap-upscaling into.
#
# What is actually being protected here, in two halves:
#
#   The value. It must equal the scale Hyprland gives eDP-1, because that is
#   exactly what it compensates for: the compositor scale the client is never
#   told about. So no case below hardcodes 2 -- each reads the host's real
#   monitor rule and expects the env var to agree. A literal that drifted from
#   laptopScale would size the UI wrongly the next time a panel changes, and the
#   failure is silent: Steam renders happily at any factor you give it.
#
#   The gate. It must be unset wherever the panel runs at scale 1. Those hosts
#   scale apps instead (hidpi.scale), so their Steam is already sized by the
#   toolkit path; forcing a second factor on top would multiply, which is the
#   double-scaling home.nix's "keep at most one of the two off 1 per host" rule
#   exists to prevent.
#
#   ./tests/steam-ui-scaling.sh            # tests this checkout
#   ./tests/steam-ui-scaling.sh /path/to/flake
set -u

FLAKE="${1:-$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)}"
[ -f "$FLAKE/flake.nix" ] || { echo "no flake.nix in: $FLAKE" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $FLAKE"

VAR=STEAM_FORCE_DESKTOPUI_SCALING
D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0

# Evaluate one option out of a host's config. nix eval's stderr is pure noise on
# a healthy box (substituter warnings, several lines per call) and the entire
# story on a broken one, so it is held back and printed only when the eval fails
# -- swallowing it outright would turn a broken checkout into a baffling
# "<unset>" that reads like a real missing value.
eval_option() { # eval_option <host> <option path>
  if ! nix eval --json "$FLAKE#homeConfigurations.$1.config.$2" 2>"$D/err"; then
    echo >&2; echo "nix eval failed for $1's $2:" >&2; cat "$D/err" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
}

# Read the var out of a host's evaluated session environment. Prints "<unset>"
# when the host does not define it, so absence is an ordinary expected value and
# not an eval failure a case has to special-case.
scaling_for() {
  eval_option "$1" home.sessionVariables \
    | jq -r --arg v "$VAR" '.[$v] // "<unset>"'
}

# The scale Hyprland gives the internal panel. hyprland.nix emits an eDP-1 rule
# only on a host whose panel wants scaling, so "no rule" is scale 1 -- the
# catch-all's value, and what that host's Steam already renders at correctly.
panel_scale_for() {
  eval_option "$1" wayland.windowManager.hyprland.settings.monitor \
    | jq -r 'map(select(.output == "eDP-1") | .scale) | (.[0] // 1) | tostring'
}

check() { # check <what> <expected> <actual>
  n=$((n+1))
  if [ "$2" = "$3" ]; then
    echo "ok   $1"
  else
    echo "FAIL $1: expected '$2', got '$3'"; fails=$((fails+1))
  fi
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for which hosts get paru, the AUR helper in home.nix's home.packages.
#
# What is actually being protected here is one predicate, `isArchHost`, and the
# reason it is not `!isDarwin`:
#
#   kyuusaku is a Linux host whose distribution is not ours -- system/deploy says
#   so in the comment above its own four-host allow-list, and refuses to converge
#   pacman there for exactly this reason. A pacman frontend in that profile is a
#   tool with no package manager under it: it evaluates, it builds, it installs,
#   and it fails at the moment somebody runs it. `!isDarwin` would put it there,
#   which is why the list is its own list and why this file exists.
#
#   mari is darwin and gets it for the more obvious reason.
#
# So every case below is about host membership, and the teeth at the end are
# about the cases themselves: a change that dropped paru from home.packages
# altogether would leave every "does not have it" case passing, which is the
# failure mode a gate test is most likely to decay into.
#
#   ./tests/aur-helper.sh            # tests this checkout
#   ./tests/aur-helper.sh /path/to/flake
set -u

FLAKE="${1:-$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)}"
[ -f "$FLAKE/flake.nix" ] || { echo "no flake.nix in: $FLAKE" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $FLAKE"

PKG=paru
D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0

# The package names in one host's profile. `pname or name` because home.packages
# holds a mix -- nixpkgs derivations, this repo's writeShellScriptBin wrappers,
# flake inputs' packages -- and not all of them carry a pname.
#
# nix eval's stderr is noise on a healthy box and the whole story on a broken
# one, so it is held back and printed only on failure. Swallowing it would turn a
# broken checkout into a host that simply "does not have paru", which is a
# passing case for five of the six hosts here.
packages_for() { # packages_for <host>
  if ! nix eval --json "$FLAKE#homeConfigurations.$1.config.home.packages" \
    --apply 'ps: builtins.map (p: p.pname or p.name or "?") ps' 2>"$D/err"; then
    echo >&2; echo "nix eval failed for $1's home.packages:" >&2; cat "$D/err" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
}

has_pkg() { # has_pkg <host>
  packages_for "$1" | jq -e --arg p "$PKG" 'any(. == $p)' >/dev/null
}

check() { # check <desc> <expected: yes|no> <host>
  n=$((n + 1))
  local desc=$1 want=$2 host=$3 got=no
  has_pkg "$host" && got=yes
  if [ "$want" = "$got" ]; then
    echo "ok   $desc"
  else
    echo "FAIL $desc: expected $PKG present=$want, got present=$got"
    fails=$((fails + 1))
  fi
}

# --- the Arch hosts ----------------------------------------------------------
# The same four system/deploy converges pacman on. They have a pacman for paru
# to drive, and they are the hosts the AUR is for.
for host in utsuho setsuna shiori fujiwara; do
  check "$host (ours, Arch) has $PKG" yes "$host"
done

# --- the hosts that must not have it -----------------------------------------
# kyuusaku is the case the predicate exists for: Linux, and not ours.
check "kyuusaku (Linux, not ours) does not have $PKG" no kyuusaku
check "mari (darwin) does not have $PKG" no mari

# --- the teeth ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Both directions have to be represented, or the suite passes having checked
# nothing. Without the first, paru removed from home.nix entirely is six green
# cases; without the second, paru handed to every host is six green cases the
# other way. The four/two split above already asserts both, so these two say it
# in the form that survives someone editing the host loops.
n=$((n + 1))
if has_pkg shiori; then
  echo "ok   at least one host still has $PKG (cases are not vacuous)"
else
  echo "FAIL no host has $PKG: every 'does not have it' case above is vacuous"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
fi

n=$((n + 1))
if has_pkg kyuusaku; then
  echo "FAIL every host has $PKG: the host gate is gone, not merely wrong"
  fails=$((fails + 1))
else
  echo "ok   at least one host still lacks $PKG (the gate is doing something)"
fi

echo
if [ "$fails" -eq 0 ]; then echo "all $n passed"; else echo "$fails of $n failed"; fi
exit $((fails > 0))
